question: What does @RequestBody do in Spring REST?
title: @RequestBody in Spring REST — JSON to Java Object Deserialization
direct_answer: **`@RequestBody`** tells Spring to deserialize the HTTP request body (JSON) into the annotated Java parameter using Jackson. The client must send `Content-Type: application/json` header. Spring calls `ObjectMapper.readValue(requestBody, ParameterType.class)` automatically.

interviewer_intent.testing: Core REST annotation — every POST/PUT endpoint uses this
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to send Content-Type: application/json header when calling the API — causes 415 Unsupported Media Type
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention @Valid with @RequestBody for automatic Bean Validation

sections.title: @RequestBody Usage
@RequestBody Key Points
sections.content:
- **Deserialization**: HTTP request body (JSON) → Java object via Jackson ObjectMapper
- **`Content-Type: application/json`**: Required header — without it, Spring returns 415 Unsupported Media Type
- **`required=true`** (default): If body is empty, Spring throws exception; `@RequestBody(required=false)` makes it optional
- **`@Valid`**: Triggers Bean Validation on the deserialized object (check @NotNull, @Size, etc.)
- **`@Validated`**: Alternative to @Valid with group support
- **`BindingResult`**: If added after @RequestBody, captures validation errors without throwing exception
- **`HttpMessageNotReadableException`**: Thrown if JSON can't be parsed to the target type
- **Customization**: Jackson annotations on the DTO class control how fields map from JSON to Java

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @RequestBody tells Spring to take the HTTP request body and deserialize it into the Java object parameter. Jackson reads the JSON from the request body and populates the Java object's fields. The client needs to set the Content-Type header to application/json — otherwise Spring returns a 415 error. A very common pattern is combining @RequestBody with @Valid for automatic input validation: if the incoming object fails validation constraints like @NotNull or @Size, Spring automatically returns a 400 Bad Request response without even reaching your method body. This is a really clean way to handle input validation without writing if-null checks everywhere.

question: What does @ResponseBody do in Spring MVC?
title: @ResponseBody in Spring MVC — Java Object to JSON Serialization
direct_answer: **`@ResponseBody`** tells Spring to serialize a controller method's return value directly to the HTTP response body (JSON) instead of treating it as a view name. In `@RestController`, `@ResponseBody` is applied automatically to all methods — you don't need to add it explicitly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of serialization direction and @ResponseBody's role
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding @ResponseBody explicitly to @RestController methods — it's already included

sections.title: @ResponseBody Explained
@ResponseBody Behavior
sections.content:
- **Without @ResponseBody**: Spring treats return value as view name → ViewResolver → HTML
- **With @ResponseBody**: Spring treats return value as data → MessageConverter (Jackson) → JSON
- **`@RestController`**: Puts @ResponseBody on ALL methods implicitly
- **Explicit use**: On individual methods in a `@Controller` for selective JSON responses
- **Content-Type header set**: Spring sets `Content-Type: application/json` when @ResponseBody produces JSON
- **Status code**: Default 200 OK — use @ResponseStatus or ResponseEntity to change
- **Null return**: If method returns null with @ResponseBody, Spring writes empty body with 200 status
- **Void return**: Returns 200 OK with no body

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @ResponseBody controls how a controller method's return value is handled. Without it, Spring assumes you're returning a view name and tries to find a matching template. With @ResponseBody, Spring takes the return value and passes it to a message converter — Jackson — to serialize it as JSON in the response body. In @RestController, @ResponseBody is automatically applied to every method, so you don't need to add it manually. The only time you'd explicitly add @ResponseBody is when you have a @Controller class that mostly returns view names, but you want a specific method to return JSON instead. It pairs directly with @RequestBody: @RequestBody deserializes incoming JSON, @ResponseBody serializes outgoing objects to JSON.

question: How do you validate a @RequestBody in Spring Boot?
title: Validating @RequestBody in Spring Boot — @Valid and Bean Validation
direct_answer: Add **`@Valid`** (or `@Validated`) before `@RequestBody` in the controller method signature. Spring runs Bean Validation (JSR-380) on the deserialized object. If validation fails, Spring throws `MethodArgumentNotValidException` and returns a `400 Bad Request` response automatically.

interviewer_intent.testing: Input validation knowledge — critical for any production API
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Manually checking fields in service layer — use Bean Validation annotations instead
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how to customize the 400 error response using @ControllerAdvice to catch MethodArgumentNotValidException

sections.title: Bean Validation with @Valid
Validation Annotations
sections.content:
- **`@NotNull`**: Field is not null
- **`@NotBlank`**: String is not null, not empty, not whitespace
- **`@NotEmpty`**: Collection or String is not null and not empty
- **`@Email`**: Valid email format
- **`@Min(value)` / `@Max(value)`**: Number range
- **`@Size(min, max)`**: String/collection length
- **`@Pattern(regexp)`**: Custom regex
- **`@Valid`**: Triggers validation; nested objects need @Valid too (cascaded validation)
- **On failure**: `MethodArgumentNotValidException` thrown → 400 Bad Request default response
- **Custom error response**: Catch `MethodArgumentNotValidException` in `@ControllerAdvice` for structured error DTO
- **Dependency**: `spring-boot-starter-validation` adds Hibernate Validator (the implementation)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: To validate a @RequestBody in Spring Boot, you add @Valid before the @RequestBody annotation and put Bean Validation annotations on your DTO class fields. Things like @NotBlank for required strings, @Email for email format, @Min and @Max for number ranges, @Size for length constraints. When the request comes in, Spring deserializes the JSON to the DTO and then validates it. If any constraint fails, Spring automatically returns a 400 Bad Request with a default error response — you don't need to write any validation logic yourself. To return a structured error response with a list of which fields failed and why, you'd add a @ControllerAdvice class with an @ExceptionHandler for MethodArgumentNotValidException to customize the error body.

question: What is @RequestHeader and @CookieValue in Spring MVC?
title: @RequestHeader and @CookieValue in Spring MVC — Header and Cookie Extraction
direct_answer: **`@RequestHeader`** extracts a specific HTTP request header value into a method parameter. **`@CookieValue`** extracts a cookie value. Both support `required=false` with `defaultValue` for optional headers/cookies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of additional Spring MVC parameter binding options
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Manually parsing HttpServletRequest for header values instead of using @RequestHeader
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that @RequestHeader can inject all headers as Map<String, String>

sections.title: @RequestHeader and @CookieValue
Header and Cookie Binding
sections.content:
- **`@RequestHeader("name")`**: Extracts single header by name; throws if required header missing
- **`@RequestHeader(required=false, defaultValue='default')`**: Optional header with fallback
- **`@RequestHeader Map<String, String>`**: Inject all headers as a map
- **`@CookieValue("name")`**: Extracts cookie value by cookie name
- **`@CookieValue(required=false)`**: Optional cookie
- **Case-insensitive**: HTTP headers are case-insensitive — Spring handles this
- **Common headers**: `Authorization`, `Content-Type`, `Accept`, `User-Agent`, `X-Request-ID`
- **vs. `HttpServletRequest`**: @RequestHeader/CookieValue is cleaner; HttpServletRequest is old style
- **JWT extraction**: Often used for extracting Bearer token from `Authorization` header (before Spring Security)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @RequestHeader lets you bind HTTP header values directly to method parameters without manually accessing HttpServletRequest. You annotate a parameter with @RequestHeader and the header name, and Spring injects the value. You can make it optional with required=false and provide a defaultValue. @CookieValue does the same for cookies. These are commonly used for things like extracting the Authorization header for a Bearer token, reading the Accept-Language header for localization, or reading a custom request ID header for tracing. A neat trick is injecting Map<String, String> with @RequestHeader to get all headers at once, useful for logging or proxy scenarios.

question: What is the difference between @RequestParam and @RequestBody?
title: @RequestParam vs @RequestBody — Query String vs JSON Body
direct_answer: **`@RequestParam`** extracts data from the **URL query string** (e.g., `/users?page=2&size=10`). **`@RequestBody`** extracts data from the **HTTP request body** (typically JSON for POST/PUT). They're used for completely different data sources.

interviewer_intent.testing: Very common confusion — choosing where to get request data from
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @RequestParam for complex objects — they should come in @RequestBody as JSON
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give clear rule: @RequestParam for simple primitive values in URL; @RequestBody for complex JSON objects in POST/PUT

sections.title: When to Use Each
Comparison
sections.content:
- **`@RequestParam`**: URL query string `?key=value`; also works for form data in non-JSON requests
- **`@RequestBody`**: HTTP request body (JSON/XML); mainly for POST, PUT, PATCH
- **GET requests**: Use @RequestParam (GET requests shouldn't have a body)
- **POST/PUT**: Use @RequestBody for complex objects; @RequestParam for optional filters
- **Data type**: @RequestParam → primitives and Strings; @RequestBody → complex POJOs
- **`@RequestParam Map<String, String>`**: Inject all query params as a map
- **Form submissions** (non-JSON): `@RequestParam` or `@ModelAttribute` — depends on content type
- **@PathVariable** vs @RequestParam: PathVariable is in the URL path (`/{id}`), RequestParam is in the query string (`?id=1`)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The key difference is where the data comes from. @RequestParam reads from the URL query string — those key-value pairs after the question mark. @RequestBody reads from the HTTP request body — the JSON payload. So for a GET endpoint with filtering and pagination, you'd use @RequestParam for the filter values and page number. For a POST endpoint creating a user, the new user's data comes as JSON in the request body, so you'd use @RequestBody to deserialize it. A simple rule: GET requests use @RequestParam or @PathVariable; POST and PUT requests use @RequestBody for the main payload and optionally @RequestParam for additional options. You can't really use @RequestBody for GET requests since GET has no body.

question: What is a DTO and why should you use it in REST APIs?
title: DTO in Spring REST — Data Transfer Object Best Practice
direct_answer: A **DTO (Data Transfer Object)** is a plain Java class designed specifically for API input/output — it contains only the fields needed for a specific request/response. Using DTOs instead of JPA entities protects internal DB structure, prevents accidental field exposure, and decouples API shape from DB schema.

interviewer_intent.testing: API design best practices — returning entities directly is a common fresher mistake
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning JPA @Entity directly from @RestController — exposes internal DB structure and causes serialization issues with lazy relationships
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that returning entity exposes all fields (including passwords), can cause Jackson serialization issues with lazy collections, and couples API to DB schema

sections.title: Entity vs DTO
Why Use DTOs
sections.content:
- **Security**: Don't expose sensitive fields (`passwordHash`, internal flags) in JSON response
- **Decoupling**: API shape can evolve independently from DB schema
- **Lazy loading**: Returning entity from @RestController can trigger LazyInitializationException on serialization
- **Jackson issues**: Bidirectional @OneToMany/@ManyToOne → infinite recursion during serialization
- **Different shapes**: Request DTO (what client sends) ≠ Response DTO (what client receives) ≠ Entity (DB structure)
- **Mapping**: Use MapStruct or manual mapping to convert Entity ↔ DTO
- **Projection**: DTOs can contain aggregated/computed fields not in the entity
- **API versioning**: Different DTO versions for v1 and v2 APIs without changing entity

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: DTOs — Data Transfer Objects — are the objects you expose through your API, as opposed to JPA entities which are tied to your database structure. Using DTOs is a best practice for several reasons. First, security: your entity might have a passwordHash or internal status fields that should never appear in the API response — a DTO lets you expose only what's appropriate. Second, lazy loading: if you return a JPA entity from a @RestController and Jackson tries to serialize it, it might hit lazy-loaded collections after the transaction has closed, causing LazyInitializationException or infinite recursion with bidirectional relationships. Third, decoupling: your API contract shouldn't change every time you rename a database column. The trade-off is the mapping code between entity and DTO, which tools like MapStruct handle efficiently.
